extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (agents and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying the 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph written description requirement and related new-matter rules in examining and prosecuting patent applications, including when rejections are appropriate and how to treat amendments, priority claims, ranges, genera/species, and incorporations by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances where written description issues arise - amendment affecting a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to the claims or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed. An amendment to the specification may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are amended or new claims added, examiners must check that the as-filed disclosure supports the change (see In re Wright). Be mindful that specification amendments (e.g., changing a term definition) can affect claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances where written description issues arise - reliance on filing date of parent application (35 U.S.C. 120)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier U.S. application only if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph in the earlier application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming priority to a parent U.S. application under 35 U.S.C. 120, ensure the earlier application provides written description support for the subject matter in question (see Tronzo v. Biomet; In re Scheiber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances where written description issues arise - reliance on foreign/provisional priority (35 U.S.C. 119)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or provisional filing date only if the corresponding foreign or provisional application supports the claims as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must verify that the foreign/provisional priority document supplies the requisite written description support for the claimed subject matter (see In re Ziegler; Kawai v. Metlesics; In re Gosteli).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances where written description issues arise - support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: In an interference, the claim corresponding to a count must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph; earlier applications relied upon must meet the 112 requirement for the subject matter of the count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad generic disclosure to a class may be insufficient for a specific compound; when benefit of an earlier-filed application is sought in interference, confirm the earlier app meets the 112 written description standard (Fields v. Conover; Hyatt v. Boone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the examiner regarding the written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry is a question of fact and a description as filed is presumed adequate unless the examiner presents sufficient evidence or reasoning to rebut the presumption. The examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of the evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy (In re Wertheim; In re Marzocchi). Do not reject absent factual findings and reasoned analysis; mere assertions of unpredictability are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of rejection requirements for lack of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which support the lack of written description conclusion: (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific findings and reasoning (MPEP §2163.04). A general allegation is not enough; a simple statement pointing out where support is absent may suffice for new/amended claims where support is not apparent. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments that can be supported, mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter (see Rasmussen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to applicant's reply on written description rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon reply by applicant, before repeating any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1, review the basis for the rejection in view of the record as a whole, including amendments, arguments, and evidence. Do not repeat the rejection if the whole record demonstrates the requirement is satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the rejection is maintained, fully respond to applicant's rebuttal and thoroughly analyze any affidavits or additional showings submitted. Failure to consider the whole record is improper (see In re Alton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to scope of claims - general support requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are broadened, narrowed, or otherwise altered (including numerical ranges or terminology changes), verify that each limitation finds support in the as-filed specification/drawings/claims (see MPEP §2163).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claim - omission of a limitation (removing an essential feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise an issue whether the inventor had possession of the broader invention; a claim that omits an element which the applicant describes as an essential or critical feature does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification indicates a feature is 'essential' or 'the only possible location' (or similar), removing it may render the claim unsupported (Gentry Gallery; Tronzo; In re Wilder). Compare cases where a limitation was not described as critical and broadening was allowed (In re Peters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claim - genus supported by species (addition of generic claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by a sufficient description of a representative number of species; when substantial variation exists, describe a sufficient variety of species. Disclosure of only one species supports a genus only if it indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess predictability and evidence that other species are operable. Single-species disclosures may suffice in predictable arts or when the disclosure indicates broader invention; otherwise, one species often won't support a genus (Enzo Biochem; In re Curtis; In re Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violates the written description requirement. A 'laundry list' of possibilities does not constitute written description of every species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgeneric terminology may or may not be acceptable; each case depends on what is reasonably communicated to those skilled in the art. Courts have found both violations and acceptances depending on facts (Fujikawa; In re Ruschig; Ex parte Sorenson; In re Smith; In re Lukach; In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Range limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing numerical range limitations, the analysis must account for which ranges a person skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that introduce an open-ended range (e.g., 'at least 35%') that reads on embodiments outside the disclosed range may fail, whereas properly bounded ranges derived from the disclosure may be acceptable (In re Wertheim; Purdue Pharma v. Faulding; Union Oil v. Atlantic Richfield). Evaluate whether the specification clearly conveys the claimed range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description requirement to new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of written description generally concerns claim subject matter. If applicant amends abstract, specification or drawings to add content not described in the application as filed, new matter arises. 35 U.S.C. 132 and 35 U.S.C. 251 prohibit introduction of new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat added content in any part of the application as potential new matter; ensure amendments do not add content beyond what was originally filed. Understand statutory prohibitions and their application to reissue and continuation contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of new matter (examiners' actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure, the examiner should object under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 and require applicant to cancel the new matter; if new matter is added to the claims, reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph - written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification is amended to add new matter affecting claim limitations, reject claims under 112, para. 1. Still consider subject matter added to the claim in making prior art rejections, since applicant may overcome a new matter rejection by amendment or argument (In re Rasmussen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of new matter objections and/or rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection of claims is reviewable by the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences, whereas an objection and requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181. If both rejection and objection occur, the issue is appealable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow proper appellate/petition channels depending on whether the examiner issues an objection (petitionable) or a rejection (appealable). Do not decide an appealable issue by petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed subject matter not disclosed in remainder of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if an originally filed claim discloses material not disclosed in the remainder of the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification, use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., Form Paragraph 7.44) and allow amendment to supply antecedent support where appropriate (In re Benno).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description - rephrasing allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere rephrasing of a passage does not constitute new matter; rewording is permissible where the same meaning remains intact. Inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at the time is not considered new matter so long as intent for a particular definition is clear from the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute terms that merely rename the invention (e.g., updated nomenclature) may be permissible (In re Anderson; Scarring Corp. v. Megan). If multiple definitions exist for a term, adding a definition requires that the as-filed disclosure make that intent clear to avoid new matter or written description issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description - correction of obvious errors
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize the existence of the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections are allowable when the correction is apparent to those skilled in the art (In re Odd). However, do not rely on foreign priority documents to support corrections in the U.S. application unless the U.S. app explicitly incorporates them by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special rules for foreign priority/incorporation for omitted portions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a foreign priority document is of record, applicant may not rely on its disclosure to support correction of an error in the pending U.S. application unless the U.S. application explicitly incorporates the foreign document by reference. For applications filed on/after Sept 21, 2004, omitted portions may be considered incorporated by reference under 37 CFR 1.55 subject to 1.57(a) conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when applicants attempt to rely on priority documents for corrections. Follow 37 CFR 1.55 and 1.57 and MPEP §201.17 for procedures and conditions for incorporation by reference of inadvertently omitted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: English translation errors in originally non-English filed U.S. applications
rubrics_metrics.description: If a U.S. application was originally filed in a non-English language and an English translation was subsequently submitted, applicant may rely on the disclosure of the originally filed non-English application to support correction of an error in the English translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translation errors exist, the original non-English filing can be used to correct the English translation; treat such corrections consistent with new matter and written description standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent function, theory, or advantage may be recited without new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: By disclosing a device that inherently performs a function or has a property, operates according to a theory or has an advantage, the application necessarily discloses that function/theory/advantage even if not stated explicitly. The application may later be amended to recite the inherent matter without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing inherency requires extrinsic evidence that 'the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present' and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; probabilities or possibilities are insufficient (In re Reynolds; In re Smythe; In re Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Information incorporated by reference is as much part of the application as if the text were repeated in the application. Replacing identified material incorporated by reference with the actual text is not new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat incorporated material as part of the application as filed. Follow 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP §608.01(p) for Office policy and procedural requirements concerning incorporation by reference.
